synopsis: Australia's model WHS Regulation 215 requires collision risks involving pedestrians and other mobile plant to be controlled so far as reasonably practicable, with a warning device where collision is possible; the model regulations bind only where adopted by a state or territory [f15531, f2256]. The research found no prescriptive Australian collision-avoidance mandate, but state-specific requirements were not found or verified, so compliance planning must check destination-state WHS adoption and mine legislation site by site [f2270, f7501, f7748, f15550]. Australia has adopted ISO 16001 as AS ISO 16001:2020 and published the modified AS 21815.1:2023 adoption of ISO 21815-1:2022, although its modifications were not verified; no identified off-road document allows simulation to replace a prescribed physical compliance test [f2179, f2721, f2872, f2103]. Reported collision burdens include 26% of Queensland mine and quarry fatalities during 1998–2016, 48 Queensland open-cut coal collisions and near misses from 1 January to 27 May 2017, and 30 NSW underground-coal LHD and personnel-transport collisions in the 12 months to mid-2025 [f3194, f3195, f3196]. Alarm burden can cause operators to ignore, bypass or switch off systems, while an acceptable false-alarm rate remains an open research question; Australian and South African guidance favors context-aware discrimination rather than universally alarming or aggressively suppressing alarms [f3303, f3019, f3621]. Australian ACARP work found that a schematic proximity display helped haul-truck simulator drivers reduce collision risk, and its test framework separates proving object detection from proving Level 8 or 9 intervention [f11837, f11752].
